title: Indian Banks Race to Raise $5 Billion in Dollars After RBI Moves FX Swap Deadline
excerpt: Private and state-run lenders are fast-tracking bond and loan issues as the central bank unexpectedly advances the end date for its concessional swap window by a month.
body:
• Indian banks are scrambling to raise at least $5 billion through dollar bonds and loans before the RBI's concessional FX swap window closes on August 31, a month ahead of schedule.
  • The scheme has already attracted over $50 billion in non-resident Indian deposits in roughly two months, bolstering India's foreign exchange reserves past $700 billion.
  • Analysts say the early closure reflects the RBI's comfort with balance-of-payments inflows and concerns about domestic liquidity management and the cost of maintaining the swap facility.

Indian banks are rushing to finalize dollar bond and loan deals over the next two weeks after the Reserve Bank of India unexpectedly advanced the deadline for its concessional foreign exchange swap facility to August 31, cutting a full month off the original September 30 timeline, according to Reuters.

Private and state-run lenders are now on track to raise at least $5 billion through a combination of overseas bonds and loans, four bankers told Reuters. The scramble comes as institutions try to lock in the RBI's subsidized hedging costs before the window shuts.

A Compressed Timeline

"Some of the fund raising plans have been brought forward to utilize the last few days," said Akshay Naik, India head of debt capital markets at Citi. "We will have one of the busiest windows for the next 6-8 days from India."

Large private-sector lenders including ICICI Bank and HDFC Bank are in talks to raise roughly $1.5 billion each through dollar bonds and loans. Axis Bank, YES Bank, RBL Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank are each planning to raise at least $500 million through overseas debt markets, according to the bankers.

State-run institutions — State Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, Canara Bank, Union Bank of India, Bank of India and Central Bank of India — are targeting raises of $250 million to $500 million each. Indian lenders have already raised $5.93 billion through dollar debt this year, with an additional $1.2 billion added last week alone.

Why the RBI Pulled the Plug Early

The swap facility was introduced in June as part of a broader package to support the rupee after it fell to record lows in May amid the Iran conflict. The scheme offered banks zero-cost hedging on foreign currency non-resident (FCNR) deposits, dramatically lowering the cost of overseas fundraising.

The strategy worked faster than expected. Non-resident Indian deposits surged past $50 billion in roughly two months, and total foreign currency inflows — including overseas borrowings — have reached nearly $57 billion, pushing India's forex reserves above $700 billion.

"Given the current pace, overseas FX deposits could reasonably reach around $70 billion by end-August. That would be roughly 10% of India's headline FX reserves and is probably a comfortable enough number for the RBI."

— Vivek Rajpal, Asia macro strategist, JB Drax Honore

Analysts at IDFC First Bank noted that allowing deposits to accumulate further could create maturity challenges three to five years out. The RBI also faces a liquidity management dilemma: as the central bank swaps dollars for rupees, excess cash in the banking system can push short-term rates below the policy rate and fan inflationary pressures.

Balance of Payments Turnaround

The deposit blitz has fundamentally altered India's external outlook. Economists who had projected a balance-of-payments deficit now expect a surplus for the fiscal year ending March 2027. Citi has trimmed its BoP surplus forecast to $53 billion from $60 billion following the early closure but still expects the rupee to find a ceiling near 95 per dollar.

The rupee slipped 0.2% to 95.60 per dollar on Monday, its weakest in two weeks, as markets digested the unexpected timeline change. Dollar-rupee forward premiums jumped, with the one-year implied yield rising 8 basis points to 2.79%.

What Comes Next

Naik at Citi expects an additional $5 billion to $7 billion in bank bond and loan issuances for the remainder of the year. Over the past 15 years, Indian banks' annual overseas borrowing has topped $6 billion only three times — including in 2013, the last time the RBI opened a similar swap window.

Bank of America analysts revised their total inflow estimate upward to $80 billion, noting "stronger than expected flows" despite the compressed window. The RBI's bet appears to be that the firewall it has built — $700 billion in reserves and a transformed BoP position — is now robust enough to weather the ongoing geopolitical turbulence without the swap subsidy.
nri_angle: NRI deposits are at the center of this story — the RBI scheme incentivized diaspora deposits and has already attracted over $50 billion from non-resident Indians in two months.
